Q: PlatformIO with Visual Studio Code and No module named 'distutils' A:

It turned out that, since I installed everything via VSCode the python version used is located in the PlatformIO folder under '~/.platformio/penv/' and the distutils are available in the setuptools pkg.

Therfore I installed it there with

source .platformio/penv/bin/activate
pip install setuptools

now it works

Q: Pylance type error when using classic `attrs` library with type comments in py 3.5 A:

This is an error that occurs at the static analysis time in Pylance, not at runtime from `attrs` or Python. The classic `attr` API on Python 3.5 does not give Pylance the information it needs to know that `_init_` was automatically generated by `@attr.s`, so it assumes that no constructor parameters are declared in the constructor of `Foo`. `_init_` cannot be inferred from `attr.ib(type=...)` because that information is not given to Pylance for constructor inference. In this context, the only actual solution is to offer the constructor under TYPE_CHECKING as you have done, or to ignore this diagnostic with # type: ignore, or to do nothing to make Pylance generate the constructor in this case.

Q: "Unable to find method org.gradle.api.internal.StartParameterInternal.getIsolatedProjects()" A:

Your Gradle is not too old. The message comes from the Kotlin Gradle plugin. The build loaded its Gradle 7.6 jar.

The base jar kotlin-gradle-plugin-<version>.jar, the one with no -gradleXX suffix, targets Gradle 7.6. Its ProjectIsolationStartParameterAccessorG76 class calls:

org/gradle/api/internal/StartParameterInternal.getIsolatedProjects:()Lorg/gradle/internal/buildoption/BuildOption$Value;

Gradle 7.6 declared Value inside BuildOption. Gradle 9.5 and 9.6 declare it inside Option, so that method no longer exists and the JVM raises NoSuchMethodError. The suffixed jars do not carry the call. I tested Kotlin 2.1.21 through 2.4.10 on Gradle 9.6.1 and each resolved a suffixed jar, so 9.6.1 is not the cause.

  1. Run ./gradlew help --stacktrace. If only the IDE sync fails, the IDE uses a different Gradle.
  2. Check the distribution in Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Build Tools | Gradle. If it names a local Gradle 9.6.1, switch back to the wrapper.
  3. Look for a jar with no -gradleXX suffix under <gradle user home>/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/org.jetbrains.kotlin/kotlin-gradle-plugin/<version>/. Gradle picks that one when the plugin reaches the build classpath as a plain library, usually through buildSrc or buildscript { classpath(...) }.
  4. Pin the wrapper to Gradle 9.5.1. The Kotlin compatibility table lists 7.6.3 to 9.5.0 for Kotlin 2.4.x, so 9.7.1 is outside the range too.

Post the --stacktrace output. It names the plugin that loads the old jar.

Q: Associative arrays: Python vs. Perl vs. AWK performace A:

When you have huge data files and you want to work with them efficiently, you're probably best off throwing them into a SQLite database, indexing them, and then querying them. See my answer about CSV vs SQLite performance for more on that.

Create a table for the data (stuff is a terrible name, but I don't know what this data is, so it's "stuff").

create table stuff (
    key1 text,
    key2 text,
    value real
);

Import your CSV files into the table using the SQLite shell:

sqlite> .mode csv
sqlite> .import file1 stuff
sqlite> .import file2 stuff
sqlite> .import file3 stuff

Create an index for the keys.

create index stuff_key on stuff (key1, key2);

Query to your heart's content.

select value
from stuff
where key1 = "NM_001011874.1" and
      key2 = "XR_104537.1"

Output:

-0.929524370261122
-0.11254525414
-0.41254525414

Once the import and indexing is done, it won't matter how large the data gets. Instead of updating the CSV files and reimporting all of them, you can import small CSV files with just the new fields. Or you can skip the CSV files and insert them directly.

insert into stuff (key1, key2, value)
values ("NM_204958293.2", "XR_29238498.3", -239.2),
       ("NM_2904892.3", "XR_3093.0", 9482.39);

I tested the performance of this, because I've advocated it a bunch of times, but haven't tested it.

First I cleared a bunch of disk space, because these files are going to get big. I'm doing this on a MacBook Pro i7 that was state of the art in 2011. Fortunately, it has an aftermarket SSD, so I/O performance is excellent. It isn't a slouch, but it's not a top of the line server either. Point is, you don't need fancy hardware to get good performance.

Then I wrote a Perl program to generate 400 million rows of data, and then while that was running, I wrote a C program to do it faster. In a rare instance of program time being more important than programmer time for a one-off script, the C program finished first winding up with two roughly identical 14 GB files. They're a bit different, but it won't matter for our purposes.

Then I created the table and started the import. The initial import time isn't terribly important because I don't have to sit here and stare at it or baby it. I know it's going to work, I know I only have to do it once, so I can work on any number of things in parallel (like editing this post). Unfortunately, SQLite isn't working in parallel, it seems to be using only one core. On the other hand, it isn't using more than about 3 MB of memory.

Importing one 400 million row file took 20 minutes. The resulting SQLite database is about 17 GB, so there isn't any great expansion of the data. I'm not going to do the rest, because it rapidly becomes redundant.

Now I'm creating the index. Again, it's a one time thing that I don't have to sit around and watch... except I do because it's using a 1 GB of virtual memory, and the SQLite file is now 30 GB. So... more deleting of files. Building the index took about 30 minutes.

50 minutes to import and index using 30 GB of disk space, about two times more than the original data. No programming is necessary.

Q: Compression to AV1 with ffmpeg, enabled --enable-libsvtav1 A:

I don't think it's just you. I've tried using the same codec to compress .png into .avif (the file size savings are completely insane), but it takes ffmpeg a REALLY long time just to compress 1 single image.

And I'm already on Apple Silicon M1 Max. As amazing and promising AV1 is to replace jpeg/png/mp4 all at once, we're still in the early phase of it, so it's gonna be a while before performance is acceptable. Nothing wrong with your parameters settings.

Heck even h.265/HEVC is still quite a bit slower than h.264/AVC at comparable crf settings, let alone AV1. I think the adoption rates for all these new algos have been distressing slow because h.264 encoding is simply too fast, while quality is "good enough" for majority of use cases.

Q: What is the earliest point at which the browser calls requestAnimationFrame? A:

After looking through section 8.12 Animation Frames, I'm not seeing an explicit description of when you can call this. Mozilla Developer Network has a good write-up; from the intro:

The window.requestAnimationFrame() method tells the browser you wish to perform an animation. It requests the browser to call a user-supplied callback function before the next repaint.

The frequency of calls to the callback function will generally match the display refresh rate. The most common refresh rate is 60hz, (60 cycles/frames per second), though 75hz, 120hz, and 144hz are also widely used. requestAnimationFrame() calls are paused in most browsers when running in background tabs or hidden <iframe>s, in order to improve performance and battery life.

Again, no indication about the earliest time you can invoke this function. A point of clarification: the browser does not call this function; your code does.

The requestAnimationFrame function exists the moment JavaScript begins executing, so you can call it. The first time the browser is capable of invoking your callback is a bit of a mystery, so I bet you'll find variance in every browser, and in between browser versions. If the specification doesn't describe it (and from what I read, it doesn't), then it's left up to the implementors to decide when; this is fancy-talk for "we don't know" and "every browser can do this differently."

The second paragraph from MDN describes a situation when requestAnimationFrame doesn't invoke a callback — scripts in a background tab or scripts running in a hidden <iframe>.

The other commentors are correct; this might be an xy problem. I suspect you are fighting something, but without seeing the code and understanding how it behaves versus how you want it to behave, I don't see how my answer will help much.

Then again, if you are genuinely curious, just try it out. Call this function at any point in the lifecycle of a web page, in multiple browsers. The worse that will happen is the callback won't get called or it will throw an error you can inspect in the developer console. The willingness to experiment and be wrong will take you a long way in your career.
